Writing a post from a Google Doc

writing-a-post-from-google-doc.Rmd
library(blogscapes)

Openscapes blog posts are drafted as a Google Doc, not directly as a Quarto .qmd file. This lets non-technical contributors write a post without touching Quarto syntax at all. google_doc_to_qmd() turns that doc into a ready-to-review index.qmd, including YAML front matter and in-body figures.

One Drive folder per post

Create one Google Drive folder per post. It should contain:

  • The Google Doc itself.
  • Every image file the post references, as plain image files (.png/.jpg/etc.) sitting in that same folder – not pasted or embedded directly into the Doc (see “Don’t paste images into the Doc” below).

google_doc_to_qmd() only needs the link to the Doc; it looks up the Doc’s own parent folder to find the images automatically.

The Doc’s metadata block

At the very top of the Doc, add a block of plain-text Field: value lines, one per line:

Blog Title: Collaboration and visioning at the 2026 ESIP Summer Meeting
Publish date:
Location: openscapes.org/blog, cross-post:
URL:
Authors: Ronny, Julie, Ileana
Image: cover.jpg
Categories: blog, ESIP, NASA, NOAA

Only Blog Title is required. Here’s what happens to each field:

Field What it becomes
Blog Title title in the YAML front matter.
Publish date date. If left blank, derived from the leading YYYY-MM-DD in the post’s folder name instead.
Location Not used in the output – informational only.
URL Ignored. citation.url is always built from base_url (an argument you pass to google_doc_to_qmd()) and the post’s folder name, since Google auto-converts a typed URL into a Markdown link that isn’t usable as a plain string. Leave this blank.
Authors Comma-separated first names (e.g. “Ronny, Julie”), matched against the package’s author table (inst/extdata/authors.csv) to produce full names and ORCID IDs in the YAML. An unrecognized name errors – add new teammates to that table first.
Image The cover image’s filename (e.g. cover.jpg). Written to the YAML as image: cover.jpg, and downloaded from the Doc’s Drive folder along with any in-body images.
Categories Comma-separated tags, written as categories: [blog, ESIP, ...]. Omitted from the YAML if left blank.

In-body images

Anywhere in the body of the post, mark where an image belongs with three consecutive plain-text lines:

image_name: data_cubes.png
caption_text: Slide from Luis Lopez' talk illustrating how virtualizing data enables people to stream data rather than downloading using current non-ARCO file structures, with the ultimate goal of AI-Ready Data Cubes
alt_text: Left-to-right workflow showing fragmented NetCDF, HDF5, and GRIB files progressing through DGGS, Zarr, VirtualiZarr, Icechunk, STAC and earthaccess, and zarr-datafusion. These technologies provide spatially consistent grids, cloud-native chunking, zero-copy access, versioning, data discovery, and efficient querying, culminating in AI-ready data cubes that require minimal preprocessing.

image_name must match a real image file in the Doc’s Drive folder. google_doc_to_qmd() replaces this three-line block with a centered Quarto figure:

::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![Slide from Luis Lopez' talk illustrating how virtualizing data enables people to stream data rather than downloading using current non-ARCO file structures, with the ultimate goal of AI-Ready Data Cubes](./data_cubes.png){fig-alt="Left-to-right workflow showing fragmented NetCDF, HDF5, and GRIB files progressing through DGGS, Zarr, VirtualiZarr, Icechunk, STAC and earthaccess, and zarr-datafusion. These technologies provide spatially consistent grids, cloud-native chunking, zero-copy access, versioning, data discovery, and efficient querying, culminating in AI-ready data cubes that require minimal preprocessing." fig-align="center" width="60%"}
:::

and downloads data_cubes.png from the Drive folder into the post folder, so the figure reference actually resolves.

You can have as many of these blocks as the post needs. If a block is missing caption_text or alt_text, or the lines aren’t consecutive, google_doc_to_qmd() leaves it as plain text and prints a message rather than failing the whole post.

Don’t paste images into the Doc

If you paste or insert an image directly into the Google Doc (instead of describing it with an image_name: block), Google’s export embeds the whole image as base64 text, producing a multi-hundred-KB unreadable .qmd. Always use an image_name: block and a real image file in the Drive folder instead.

Generating the post 

google_doc_to_qmd(
  doc = "https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QY_OrDsVcWy25eP8JmYAaRCegSsjprr9Jwz_fbAbUBw/edit",
  post_name = "2026-09-09-openscapes_esip_summer_2026",
  blog_dir = "website-new/blog",
  base_url = "https://openscapes.org/blog/"
)

This downloads the Doc, builds the YAML front matter, converts any image_name: blocks, downloads the referenced images from the Doc’s Drive folder, and writes everything to website-new/blog/2026-09-09-openscapes_esip_summer_2026/index.qmd.

post_name must start with a YYYY-MM-DD date (- or _ separated) – it’s used both as the post’s folder name and, if the Doc’s Publish date was left blank, as the source of the YAML date.

Re-downloading images only

If you replace an image file in the Drive folder after already running google_doc_to_qmd(), you don’t need to regenerate the whole post – download_doc_images() fetches just the images:

download_doc_images(
  doc = "https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QY_OrDsVcWy25eP8JmYAaRCegSsjprr9Jwz_fbAbUBw/edit",
  image_names = c("cover.jpg", "data_cubes.png"),
  post_dir = "website-new/blog/2026-09-09-openscapes_esip_summer_2026"
)

Before crossposting

Once the .qmd looks right, review it like any other pull request. Then use verify_post_images() and crosspost_blog() to copy it into other Openscapes-affiliated repositories – see the “Crossposting a post” vignette.
